A word can be kiln-keyed to a second wor.why: "Kiln-keyed" is a made-up relation between words (catalogued as kiln_keyed_to, fictional, no property tags): nothing in everyday English gives it a direction or a chaining sense, unlike 'derives from' or 'is descended from', so a model has no default reading of it as transitive or not. It could exist unrecorded as a niche lexicographers' label, which is why it is a made-up relation and not a made-up fact.

notes: RBox expansion paired with grammar-replace-0009 (the revision makes 'derives from' non-transitive: a word can derive from a second word that derives from a third without deriving from the third). Here a made-up relation, 'is kiln-keyed to', gets the same property, applied to real word pairs (coffee, koffie, kahve and alcohol); the instances differ from the revision's (sugar, nāranj). The prompts give both links, so the answer rests on the inserted property, not on etymology. Yes and no: the direct question and the first instance (asked in Chinese and Spanish too) go no, the second instance asks whether the chain could fail (yes); the topic's other RBox expansions supply the yes directs. Near asks transitivity of a real relation whose answer is yes, so an edit that spreads non-transitivity to other relations is caught; far is an unrelated transitive comparison. The coined term stays untranslated in the cross-lingual prompts.
